meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('I') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: I won a lucky ticket.
No, I am not running away.
Do you feel bad with me right now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (root 'играть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to win', forming an aspectual pair with 'выигрывать'.

examples.trans: I won a lucky ticket.
You won't win this election.
We won!

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'happy', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: I won a lucky ticket.
I'm very happy.
The film has a happy ending.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'ticket', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: I won a lucky ticket.
Listen here, we bought tickets after all!

examples.text: Я купил два билета в кино.
examples.trans: I bought two tickets to the cinema.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'when'.

examples.trans: When do new relationships begin?
When I grow up, I'll be the mayor.
Oh yeah? When?

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (root 'рождаться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to new'.

examples.trans: When do new relationships begin?
I won a lucky ticket.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'new', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: When do new relationships begin?
We need to introduce a new menu.
A new house.

meanings.note: Verbal action or result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание', meaning 'attitude' in conversational and formal Russian.

examples.trans: When do new relationships begin?

examples.text: А я испорчу отношения с будущим мэром.
examples.trans: And I'll ruin my relationship with the future mayor.
We have a very warm relationship.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.

examples.trans: Then a bright flame flares up.
He received a suspended sentence back then.
Then they will definitely lock German up fast.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'bright', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Then a bright flame flares up.
I won a lucky ticket.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'bright', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: Then a bright flame flares up.

examples.text: Я просто хотел добавить яркий аромат.
examples.trans: I simply wanted to add a vivid aroma.

examples.text: Что это за странная яркая бумага?
examples.trans: What is this strange bright paper?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'flares', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Then a bright flame flares up.
Over time a flame can go out.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'with' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: Over time a flame can go out.
Do you feel bad with me right now?
I feel very good with you.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'time', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Over time a flame can go out.

examples.text: Слушайте, а Герман всё время пьёт таблетки.
examples.trans: Listen, German is taking pills all the time.
I don't have time.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('maybe') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Maybe you could help?
Maybe tomorrow.
I thought maybe you wouldn't see me.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (root 'тухнуть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to out'.

examples.trans: Over time a flame can go out.
I won a lucky ticket.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: But just one spark is enough.
But suddenly a cook walked in there.

examples.text: Но достать её придётся тебе самой.
examples.trans: But you will have to get it out yourself.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'enough'.

examples.trans: But just one spark is enough.
That is quite enough.
That is quite enough for you.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'only'.

examples.trans: But just one spark is enough.
And we are only dating starting today.
I only need the watermelon pulp.

meanings.note: Everyday conversational Russian num meaning 'one', frequent in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Look, there is one more video clip.
Give me just one.
I have one brother.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'enough', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: But just one spark is enough.
I won a lucky ticket.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Are you running away again today?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.trans: Are you running away again today?
And we are only dating starting today.
Today will be our first day.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'again'.

examples.trans: Are you running away again today?

examples.text: Но он опять сделает вам плохо.
examples.trans: But he will hurt you again.

examples.text: Подожди, что значит это слово опять?
examples.trans: Wait, what does that word 'again' mean?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (root 'бегать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to run away', forming an aspectual pair with 'убежать'.

examples.trans: Are you running away again today?
No, I am not running away.
I am not going to run away.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('no') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, I am not running away.

examples.text: Говори, у меня от коллег нет секретов.
examples.trans: Speak, I have no secrets from colleagues.

examples.text: Нет его там в нашем списке.
examples.trans: He is not there on our list.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('not') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, I am not running away.
Chef, come on, do not keep us in suspense.

examples.text: Герман ни в чём не виноват.
examples.trans: German is not to blame for anything.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.

examples.trans: Everything is just happening so fast.
He is just a total psycho!
Katyusha, I beg you, just calm down.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.trans: Everything is just happening so fast.
Good morning to all of you.
Thank you, everything is very tasty.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything is just happening so fast.

examples.text: Его так легко вывести из себя?
examples.trans: Is it that easy to make him lose his temper?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'fast'.

examples.trans: Everything is just happening so fast.
I will slice everything up quickly right now.

examples.text: А потом они решили быстро уехать.
examples.trans: And then they decided to leave quickly.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (root 'исходить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to happen', forming an aspectual pair with 'произойти'.

examples.trans: Everything is just happening so fast.
What is going on? I don't understand.
What is happening here?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'now'.

examples.trans: Do you feel bad with me right now?
We have a lot of work right now.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'badly'.

examples.text: Значит, Герману без них будет плохо.
examples.trans: That means German will feel bad without them.

examples.text: Но он опять сделает вам плохо.
examples.trans: But he will hurt you again.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.

examples.trans: I feel very good with you.
Well, there is a very long story there.
We have been friends for a very long time.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'well'.

examples.trans: I feel very good with you.

examples.text: Феде сейчас так хорошо от таблеток.
examples.trans: Fedya feels so good from the pills right now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (root 'сить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to ask', forming an aspectual pair with 'попросить'.

examples.trans: Katya, I beg you, stay.

examples.text: Денис, я же срочно просила арбуз.
examples.trans: Denis, I urgently asked for watermelon.
Katyusha, I beg you, just calm down.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to remain', forming an aspectual pair with 'оставаться'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Katya, I beg you, stay.
There's nothing left.
I'll stay at home.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('all right') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: All right, I will stay a little longer.
All right, let's go have breakfast together.

examples.text: Ладно, спасибо, ты мне поднял настроение.
examples.trans: All right, thanks, you lifted my spirits.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'more'.

examples.trans: All right, I will stay a little longer.
Look, there is one more video clip.

examples.text: Я ещё раз спрашиваю, где мой нож?
examples.trans: I am asking once again, where is my knife?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'a little'.

examples.trans: I need to do a bit of work.

examples.text: Мы даём вам ещё немного времени.
examples.trans: We are giving you a little more time.

побыть.gloss: to stay for a while, to be (briefly)

meanings.en: to stay for a while, to be (briefly)
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (root 'быть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to stay for a while', forming an aspectual pair with 'быть'.

examples.trans: All right, I will stay a little longer.
I want to be alone.
Let's stay here a little longer.
